details:
**The Jungle Book**
Kipling's 1894 collection of stories set mostly in the Indian jungle and his most common giveaway. Its central figure is Mowgli, a "man-cub" raised by wolves, alongside the bear Baloo, the panther Bagheera, the python Kaa, and the wolf-pack leader Akela.

**Mowgli and Shere Khan**
Mowgli is the human boy raised by the Seeonee wolf pack in The Jungle Book. His great enemy is the tiger Shere Khan, who wants to kill him; in "Kaa's Hunting," Mowgli is kidnapped by the Bandar-log (monkey people) and rescued by Kaa, Baloo, and Bagheera.

**"Rikki-Tikki-Tavi" and Nag and Nagaina**
A Jungle Book story about a young mongoose adopted by an English family in India. He protects the boy Teddy and his parents from the cobras Nag and Nagaina, killing Nag and then chasing Nagaina into her hole after she bargains for her last egg; the tailorbird Darzee and his wife help him.

**"Gunga Din"**
A poem from Barrack-Room Ballads, told by a British soldier in India in Cockney dialect, about an Indian water-carrier (bhisti) whom the soldiers mock and beat. Gunga Din saves the speaker's life and is shot dead, and the poem ends, "You're a better man than I am, Gunga Din!"

**"Lazarushian-leather" and "squidgy-nosed old idol"**
Mocking descriptions of Gunga Din's skin and appearance used by the speaker, who also says that "for all 'is dirty 'ide, / 'E was white, clear white, inside." Gunga Din carries a goatskin water-bag as his only equipment.

**"The White Man's Burden"**
Kipling's 1899 imperialist poem urging the United States to colonize the Philippines. It opens many stanzas with "Take up the White Man's burden," tells readers to "send forth the best ye breed," and calls the colonized "new-caught, sullen peoples, / Half devil and half child"; it was widely parodied, including by critics who asked about "the brown man's burden."

**"If—"**
A poem of advice addressed to a son (inspired by his son John), first published in Rewards and Fairies after the story "Brother Square-Toes." It opens "If you can keep your head when all about you / Are losing theirs and blaming it on you," calls Triumph and Disaster "two impostors," urges the reader to "fill the unforgiving minute / With sixty seconds' worth of distance run," and ends "you'll be a Man, my son!"

**"Recessional"**
A hymn-like poem written for Queen Victoria's 1897 Diamond Jubilee warning against imperial pride. It addresses the "God of our fathers, known of old, / Lord of our far-flung battle-line," declares that "all our pomp of yesterday / Is one with Nineveh and Tyre," and repeats the refrain "Lest we forget—lest we forget!"

**Kim**
Kipling's 1901 novel about Kimball O'Hara, an orphan of Irish parentage in Lahore known as "Little Friend of all the World." He travels with the Tibetan lama Teshoo Lama, who seeks the River of the Arrow, while being trained as a British spy (by Mr. Lurgan, who teaches him the memory game now called "Kim's Game") in the "Great Game" against Russia, alongside agent Hurree Babu.

**"Mandalay"**
A poem in which a British soldier back in rainy London longs for a Burmese girl he met "by the old Moulmein Pagoda" in Burma. Its refrain is "On the road to Mandalay, / Where the flyin'-fishes play," and the speaker wishes to be shipped "somewheres east of Suez, where the best is like the worst" and "there aren't no Ten Commandments."

**"The Man Who Would Be King"**
A story in which two British adventurers, Daniel Dravot and Peachey Carnehan, tell a journalist narrator that "India is not big enough" and go to remote Kafiristan, where Dravot is worshipped as a god and descendant of Alexander the Great. The scheme collapses when his bride bites him and he bleeds, proving he is human, and he is killed.

**Captains Courageous**
Kipling's 1897 novel about Harvey Cheyne, a spoiled rich American boy who is washed off an ocean liner and rescued by Manuel, a Portuguese fisherman from the Gloucester fishing schooner We're Here. Working on the boat over the season transforms him.

**"Danny Deever"**
A Barrack-Room Ballads poem about the execution of a British soldier by hanging in front of his regiment. It is a dialogue in which Files-on-Parade asks the Colour-Sergeant questions like "What makes you look so white?"

**Just So Stories and other Jungle Book tales**
Just So Stories is a collection of humorous pourquoi (origin) tales; in "How the First Letter Was Written," the girl Taffimai Metallumai sends a picture message to her mother. Other Jungle Book tales include "The White Seal," about Kotick seeking a safe beach for seals away from Novastoshnah, and "Toomai of the Elephants," about a boy and the elephant Kala Nag.

**"The Female of the Species" and other poems**
"The Female of the Species" claims that "the female of the species is more deadly than the male." Kipling also wrote "The Gods of the Copybook Headings" (included in T. S. Eliot's 1941 selection of his verse) and "The Rowers," which helped popularize "Hun" as an insult for Germans.
